In Bhadrachalam's only English-medium school, everyone knew Francis and Nandini would fight for the science exhibition slot at district level. When Francis's rain-gauge model was picked, the whispers began within a week.

"Sir, his model is the same as one on a video site," Nandini told the physics teacher in the corridor, loudly enough for the Class 9 line to hear. By Friday two of Francis's friends were asking if it was true.

Francis's first thought was to tell everyone about the time Nandini's project leaned on her brother's help. He sat on the temple steps near his house that evening and let the idea go.

On Monday he carried his rough notebook to the staffroom: three weeks of sketches, the failed funnel design, the bill for the plastic tubing from Raju's hardware shop. "Sir, I heard there's doubt about my model. These are my drafts." The teacher turned the pages slowly and nodded.

Francis didn't say one word about Nandini.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?

At the swim club in Busan, Layla noticed the change before anyone said anything. Coach Park stopped giving her the fast lane. Two girls from the relay team went quiet when she walked into the changing room.

It was Jin. Layla found out from a younger swimmer: Jin had been telling people that Layla skipped the dawn sessions and only turned up for time trials. It wasn't true. Layla had missed one Tuesday, for a dentist visit, and had told the front desk.

That night she wanted to message the whole team about Jin's own late arrivals. She typed it out. Then she deleted it.

The next morning, before warm-up, she asked Coach Park for two minutes. "I heard there's a worry that I miss dawn sessions. I've only missed one this term. The front desk has the sign-in sheet." The coach checked it that afternoon.

Layla kept arriving at five-forty, every day, and kept swimming. The lane came back the following week.

The selection trial for the district hockey squad was at seven, and it was pouring. Leela's bus had broken down near the flyover, so she ran the last kilometre with her stick wrapped in a plastic bag.

She arrived soaked and three minutes late. Preeti, stretching near the goal, didn't lower her voice. "Relax, she'll get picked anyway. Her mama is on the committee."

Leela felt it in her throat. The worst part was that she had wondered the same thing. Her uncle did sit on the committee. She hadn't asked him for anything, but maybe he had said something.

She had no time to argue, and she didn't try. She played the trial on a waterlogged pitch, went hard into every tackle, and kept her mouth shut.

Afterwards she walked up to Coach Rehana. "Ma'am, can you tell me honestly where my game is? Not what my family would want to hear." The coach looked at her for a long moment. "Your tackling is squad level. Your passing under pressure isn't yet. Work on that."

The notice went up on Monday: Sangeeta, editor, school magazine. By lunch, Mridul was holding court at the canteen counter.

"Obviously she got it. Her mother teaches chemistry here. Principal Sir loves her." He saw Sangeeta coming and grinned wider. "Congratulations, editor. Well connected."

Sangeeta paid for her samosa and walked away without a word, though her ears were burning. Mridul wasn't entirely stupid. She did sometimes wonder whether her mother's name had helped.

That evening in their flat in Lajpat Nagar, she sat staring at the three pieces she had submitted. Were they good, or just familiar?

Sangeeta went home and started rewriting the poem. She didn't reply to Mridul's comments in the group chat.

The coaching institute's brochure lay on the dining table in the Kothrud flat, the engineering entrance batch circled in red by Papa. Sumit's elder sister Anjali watched him flip it open and close it again.

"You'll join, na?" Mummy asked from the kitchen. "Papa has already spoken to them."

"Yes, Mummy." He said it the way he had said it since Class 8. He loved them. He also knew the quiet that would fall over dinner if he said anything else.

Sumit was quiet. "I like making things. I like the design club. I don't know if that's engineering or something else."

"Then find out before you sign up for two years of it. Talk to them. Papa listens more than you think."

That night Sumit wrote two lists: what he enjoyed and what he feared. On Sunday, over breakfast, he asked his parents if they could talk about both before he joined.

Come, Dilnaz, sit. You think you are the first girl in this family to fight about her future? Let me tell you about Class 10.

I wanted to paint. Not a hobby. A career. My Abba wanted me to be a teacher like my aunt. For months I screamed at him, locked my door, and once I told him I was at a friend's house studying when I was really at the art school on Mall Road. He found out. That lie hurt him more than any shouting.

I still remember my guilt, sitting on the stairs that night. I loved him, and I was so angry with him.

So I changed. I gathered every drawing I'd done that year into one folder. I found out the art school's fees and scholarship dates. I told him I would finish my teacher's training too, as a backup. He took the folder to his room and didn't come out for an hour.

I, Sharmila, did both, and I painted for forty years.

Before. At Diwali, Pradeep's mother, Chandrika, told every aunty at the gathering, "Pradeep will crack the top engineering college, no doubt." He smiled and passed the sweets. His collar felt tight.

During. Three weeks later he got his half-yearly maths paper back: 41 out of 80. He folded it into his geometry box and did not show it to anyone. That night he lay awake picturing his mother's face at the next family call, telling everyone again. He thought about just not mentioning it, maybe forging the signature.

After. On Sunday morning, while she was chopping onions, he stood by the kitchen door. "Amma, I got 41 in maths. I didn't want to tell you. When you say those things to everyone, it feels really heavy. I like that you believe in me. I just can't carry all of it."

Chandrika put down the knife. She was quiet a long time. "I'll stop announcing things," she said. "Show me the paper. We'll find you help."

qa.a: Pradeep got 41 out of 80.

Vaibhav, you think your Papa is too proud of you? Let me tell you about mine. I'm your Tarun Chacha, and when I was fifteen, my father told the whole mohalla I would be the first doctor in the family.

Every time he said it at the paan shop, I felt a stone on my chest. I was not a bad student, but I wasn't that good in chemistry. In Class 11 I failed the first unit test. Failed. I hid the answer sheet under my mattress for a month.

Then it came out at the parent-teacher meeting, in front of my father and my teacher. He didn't shout. He looked tired, and that was worse.

On the walk home I told him, "Baba, I love that you believe in me. But when you tell everyone I'll be a doctor, I feel I'm not allowed to fail." He stopped walking. After that, he still said he was proud of me, but he stopped announcing my future.

qa.a: Telling his Baba on the walk home how heavy the praise felt was the turning point, because it replaced hiding with honesty and changed how his father talked.

Thursday night

Abbu came home at eleven again, smelling of the bakery ovens, and fell asleep in his chair with his shoes on. He took the second shift so I could stay at this school. Everyone knows. He tells me whenever I skip revision: "I stand at that oven for you, Harish beta."

I told Asif at lunch that I want to study design, not medicine, and Asif said, "Then tell your Abbu, idiot. He's working for you to have choices, na?"

Maybe. Tonight I made a plan. I'll keep my marks up, properly, no shortcuts. And on Sunday, when he's not tired, I'll show him the design course list and tell him the truth. I want to honour what he's doing. I just don't think that means living a life I didn't choose.

Gautam's father ran the fertiliser shop on the main road of Sehore, and every customer knew Gautam was supposed to top Class 10. When the half-yearly results came, he had come ninth.

"Just keep the card in your bag," his cousin Abhinav said on the bus home. "Tell Chacha the school is sending it next week. By then the finals will fix it."

Gautam watched the fields go by. His throat felt thick. Hiding it would buy a week. It would also mean lying every evening at the shop.

He got off at the stop and walked straight into the shop, past the sacks. "Papa, my result." His father read it standing at the counter, slowly.

"Ninth." Papa let out a long breath. "I expected more."

"Me too, Papa. I didn't understand accounts at all. Can Sharma Sir's evening class take me?"

Papa was silent, then said, "Ninth is not the end. We'll ask him tomorrow."

Kaito and Nadia were sitting on the swings in the park behind their block in Osaka, their school bags in the sand, when Nadia said, "Can I tell you something? You can't laugh."

"I won't."

"My parents are separating. Dad's moving out next month. I've known since summer." She pulled at a thread on her sleeve. "I haven't told anyone."

Kaito felt proud she had picked him, and scared he would say the wrong thing. He almost made a joke about the loud neighbours to lighten it, then stopped. "That sounds really hard. Thanks for telling me."

They swung slowly for a while.

"Please don't tell the others at school."

"I won't. It's yours to tell." He paused. "Have you talked to any adult about how you're feeling? Like your aunt, or Ms Tanaka?"

"Not really."

"Maybe your aunt? You said she's easy to talk to."

Nadia nodded. "I'll call her tonight."

"I'll walk you to her office after assembly, if you want."

"…Okay."

passage:
I'm Samir, and in Class 10 I was the one who always had to know everything. So when Jahnavi started leaving school early every Thursday, I couldn't let it go.

"Where do you go?" I asked. "Dentist? Tuition?" She said, "Just family stuff." That should have been enough. It wasn't. I asked her cousin. I checked who picked her up. I even asked her in front of the others once, "Is someone sick at your place?" She went red and walked off.

That night I felt awful. I realised I didn't actually want to help her. I wanted to be the one who knew. That's not friendship. That's collecting.

The next day I said, "I'm sorry I kept asking. You don't owe me anything. If you ever want to talk, I'm around. If not, that's fine too."

Two months later, on a bus ride, she told me her grandmother had been having therapy at the hospital on Thursdays. I never told anyone. It wasn't mine to tell.

qa.q: What day did Jahnavi leave school early?
qa.a: Jahnavi left school early every Thursday.

qa.q: What did Samir realise that night that made Samir feel awful?
qa.a: Samir felt ashamed on realising the questions came from wanting to be the one who knew, not from wanting to help Jahnavi.

qa.q: What did Samir do the next day that helped?
qa.a: Samir apologised for prying and told Jahnavi she did not owe any explanation, leaving room for her to share at her own pace.

qa.q: What was it like for Jahnavi when Samir asked in front of the others?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt embarrassed and exposed, which is why she went red and walked away.

grounding: It shows a teen who keeps prying into a friend's private matters to be in the know, then stops and lets her share at her own pace.

Class teacher's note, 9C, second week of February

I have been watching Ramesh closely since Akash's attendance dropped. Akash has missed four Mondays this term. Ramesh has asked him about it at least daily: "Where were you? Is your father in trouble? Did you move?" On Friday, Ramesh told the class chat group that Akash's family was "having court problems." Akash had told him nothing of the kind; Ramesh had guessed.

Akash was very quiet on Saturday and ate lunch alone.

I spoke to Ramesh after class. I did not accuse him. I asked why he needed to know so badly. He shrugged, then said, "Everyone asks me what's going on. I like knowing." I asked how he'd feel if someone posted guesses about his family. He was silent for a while.

He deleted the message himself and, on Monday, apologised to Akash in front of me. I have told Akash that he can talk to me or the counsellor any time, and I will call his parents this week to check in.

qa.q: How many Mondays has Akash missed this term?
qa.a: Akash has missed four Mondays this term.

qa.q: Why did Ramesh keep asking Akash questions?
qa.a: Ramesh enjoyed feeling important and in the know, which made him curious and pushy about Akash's private life.

qa.q: How did the class teacher help Ramesh see the harm?
qa.a: The teacher asked, without accusing, how Ramesh would feel if someone posted guesses about his family, which let him see it himself.

qa.q: What was it like for Akash when the guess spread in the class chat?
qa.a: Akash seemed hurt and embarrassed, going very quiet and eating lunch alone the next day.

grounding: It shows a teen who keeps prying into a friend's private matters to be in the know, the harm of sharing guesses, and learning to let the friend share at their own pace.
